next: the next check runs about 1 PM; a fresh discussion this evening, sooner if the channel at Caltrain passes Flood Monitoring or the models jump again
headline: The front is here and the channel at Caltrain is rising fast (2.08 ft, Monitoring is 2.8 ft); the HRRR backed off its noon cell, but RRFS and NBM came up, so the consensus for the wettest 3 hours is now about 1.0 in, solidly Yellow.

summary.text: Models swapped places: HRRR fell from 1.37 to 0.61 in for the wettest 3 hours (no more 1-inch hour), while RRFS rose from 0.61 to 1.14 in and NBM from 0.79 to 0.99 in. Consensus rose 0.79 → 0.99 in.
Wettest 3 hours from 10 AM: RRFS 1.14 in, NBM 0.99, ECMWF 0.70, HRRR 0.61. RRFS is the wet outlier with 0.68 in from 1 to 2 PM. Consensus (HRRR ×1.25, RRFS, NBM: middle value) 0.99 in.
Most likely water across the yards toward the garage doors (Yellow) at the peak. Red needs about 1.2 in in 3 hours; the RRFS (1.14 in) is just short of it.
Heaviest rain most likely 10 AM to 3 PM: HRRR and NBM peak 10 AM–1 PM, RRFS 12–3 PM. Second round of showers and possible thunderstorms after midnight and again Thursday late morning.
The Bay is falling toward a 1:23 PM low (2.8 ft predicted, model about 4.2 ft, ~1.4 ft surge), so drainage improves through the burst. Caltrain channel gauge rose about 1 ft in the last 40 minutes.
Cars out of the cul-de-sac now if not already. Keep the dashboard open until about 3 PM and take timestamped photos of the street at the peak.

sections.title: Synopsis
sections.text: The cold front is crossing the Peninsula now; NWS San Francisco's 10 AM aviation update has the boundary passing SFO around 10 AM, with steady rain turning more showery this afternoon and evening. NWS issued a Flood Advisory for urban and small-stream flooding across the Bay Area (including Redwood City) until 11:45 AM, noting 0.5 to 1 in had already fallen and another 0.2 to 0.5 in expected. Behind the front, colder air and a surface low bring showers and isolated thunderstorms tonight into Thursday morning. NWS storm totals through Friday morning are unchanged: 1.5–2.5 in for most of the Bay Area. A weaker front follows Saturday into Sunday.

sections.title: What changed and model trends
sections.text:
Since the 1 AM discussion the models traded places. The HRRR (8 AM run) dropped its big noon cell: the wettest 3 hours from now are 0.61 in (10 AM–1 PM) with no hour above 0.31 in, down from 1.37 in and a 1.05 in hour. The HRRR 15-minute feed has the wettest quarter-hour at 0.15 in ending 11:30 AM. Meanwhile the RRFS (10 PM run, now about 12 hours old) came up from 0.61 to 1.14 in (noon–3 PM), with 0.68 in in the hour from 1 to 2 PM, and NBM rose from 0.79 to 0.99 in (10 AM–1 PM). ECMWF is 0.70 in. GFS matches HRRR here because it blends HRRR in the first hours.

The dashboard's consensus (HRRR ×1.25 = 0.76, RRFS 1.14, NBM 0.99; middle value) is 0.99 in, up from 0.79 in, solidly in Yellow and below Red (about 1.18 in). The RRFS 0.68 in hour would also trip the 1-hour rule (0.40 in or more means at least Yellow). The HRRR has under-forecast our big bursts before, so I'd treat its 0.61 in as low; the RRFS can overdo convective cells, so 1.14 in is a reasonable upper middle. I think the consensus is about right.

Storm totals for the next 72 hours: RRFS 2.49 in, NBM 2.21, GFS 2.13, HRRR 2.02, ECMWF 1.95.

sections.title: Tide and the channel
sections.text:
This morning's 7.0 ft high tide (7:21 AM predicted) ran higher on NOAA's Bay model, near 8.9 ft around 7:55 AM, about 1.9 ft of surge. The tide is now falling toward a predicted 2.8 ft low at 1:23 PM; the Bay model holds it near 4.2 ft at 1 PM, about 1.4 ft above normal, so drainage during the midday burst is better than at dawn but still slowed. Tonight's high is 6.2 ft at 6:57 PM (model about 7.8 ft), and Thursday's 7.4 ft high at 7:58 AM shows about 9.7 ft on the model (roughly 2.3 ft of surge). The Coastal Flood Advisory now runs until 10 AM Friday.

Channel: the gauge upstream of Caltrain is reporting often today and is rising quickly: 1.04 ft at 9:29 AM, 1.46 ft at 9:50 and 2.08 ft at 10:08 AM. County Flood Monitoring there is 2.8 ft (Watch 4.1, Warning 5.5). At that pace it could reach Monitoring within the hour if the heavy rain keeps up. At Alameda de las Pulgas the channel rose from 0.42 ft at 9 AM to 1.14 ft at 10 AM (Monitoring 3.18 ft).

sections.title: Current observations
sections.text: Rain is under way and picked up after 9 AM. The rain gauge at Caltrain had 0.56 in in the last 24 hours as of 9:42 AM, 0.32 in in the last 3 hours and 0.12 in in the last hour, with 0.20 in in the 9 AM hour, the wettest so far. The first channel rise came with the frontal rain around 5:45 AM (Caltrain gauge 0.07 to 1.04 ft), it eased after 7 AM, and the second, faster rise began about 9:30 AM.

sections.title: Uncertainty
sections.text: Moderate to high. The wettest-3-hour spread is 0.61 to 1.14 in, and the HRRR and RRFS have swapped roles between runs, which usually means the models can't place the heaviest cells along the front. The RRFS run is about 12 hours old; newer runs could move it either way. Any embedded thunderstorm can drop 0.5 in in 20–30 minutes. Most likely outcome: Yellow at the peak. Red (about 1.2 in in 3 hours) needs the RRFS's 1–2 PM burst to verify over us. The fast channel rise is the thing to watch: a channel at county levels slows street drainage no matter what the rain does.

sections.title: What to do now
sections.text:
• Move cars out of the cul-de-sac now if they are still there.
• If it's safe, clear leaves from the street drain grates and yard drains during a lull; strong south winds are still bringing leaves down.
• Gusty winds can cause power outages, and the pump station needs power. If the power goes out during heavy rain, assume the pumps may be slow and watch the street.
• Keep the dashboard open until about 3 PM: the 1-hour burst alarm and the channel levels need live readings.
• At the peak, take a photo of the street with the time visible.
• Plan for a second round after midnight and Thursday late morning.
• Don't drive or walk through moving water.
